Text Mining and Sentiment Analysis of U.S. Presidential Inaugural Addresses

Text mining · Regular expressions · Word clouds · Sentiment analysis · Machine learning · Statistical testing

Summary

Political speeches are public, carefully written texts. This notebook mines all 60 U.S. inaugural addresses (1789–2025) from NLTK's public-domain inaugural corpus and asks how the language of the presidency has changed.

# Question Method
1 Which words characterise each historical era? Regex cleaning, stop-word removal, word clouds, weighted log-odds
2 How has speaking style changed? Sentence length, lexical diversity, "we" vs "I", Spearman trend tests
3 How positive or negative is the language, and has it changed? VADER on 3-sentence passages, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kruskal–Wallis test, sensitivity to passage size
4 Can a bag-of-words model predict that sentiment, and what does it learn? Grouped cross-validation, model comparison, nested threshold tuning, temporal hold-out
5 How far can the sentiment labels be trusted? A blind human-labelling step with Cohen's κ (see Section 8)

Design decisions that matter

  • No human labels exist, so VADER (a rule-based tool) labels each passage. A model trained on those labels shows agreement with VADER, not accuracy against human judgment. Section 8 adds a small human check, and Section 9 compares model and VADER against it.
  • Splits are grouped by speech. Passages from one speech share topics and wording, so spreading them across train and test would inflate scores.
  • Threshold tuning is nested. The decision threshold is chosen only on training folds, so the reported score is not optimistic.
  • Negations survive stop-word removal for the sentiment model ("not good" is not "good").
  • Honest uncertainty. Trends get test statistics, era differences get confidence intervals, and claims that rest on 60 speeches are worded accordingly.

Data: the inaugural corpus of NLTK, one text file per address (e.g. 1861-Lincoln.txt), downloaded automatically.

What is VADER? Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner is a rule-based tool. A dictionary gives each word a sentiment score (hope is positive, war is negative), and simple rules adjust for negation ("not good"), intensifiers ("very good"), capitalisation and exclamation marks. It returns a compound score from −1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive) and needs no training, but it can miss irony and context, and was built for modern informal text.

Each file in the corpus is one address. The file name holds the year and the speaker, which gives two metadata columns for free. The DataFrame speeches built here is the single source of truth: later cells add columns to it but never replace it.

3. Regular expressions and text cleaning

Regular expressions (regex) are patterns for finding and rewriting text. First they explore the raw speeches, then they clean them.

3.1 Exploring with regex

The patterns below count years, forms of address, contractions and two themes. Counts become a rate per 1,000 words, so long and short speeches can be compared.

3.2 Cleaning with regex

The cleaning function applies these steps in order:

  1. lower-case everything,
  2. unify curly apostrophes and expand contractions (can't → cannot), so that negations survive,
  3. drop the possessive 's,
  4. replace everything that is not a letter or digit (punctuation, dashes) by a space,
  5. collapse repeated whitespace.

Sentences are split before cleaning, because cleaned text has no punctuation left. The splitter masks abbreviations such as "Mr." so they are not read as sentence ends. Small assert tests make the behaviour explicit and protect against regressions.

In [4]
CONTRACTIONS = [
    (r"\bwon't\b", "will not"),
    (r"\bcan't\b", "cannot"),
    (r"\bain't\b", "is not"),
    (r"\blet's\b", "let us"),
    (r"\b(it|he|she|that|there|here|what|who|where|how)'s\b", r"\1 is"),
    (r"n't\b", " not"),
    (r"'re\b", " are"),
    (r"'ve\b", " have"),
    (r"'ll\b", " will"),
    (r"'d\b", " would"),
    (r"'m\b", " am"),
]

def clean_text(text):
    text = text.lower().replace("’", "'")
    text = re.sub(r"https?://\S+|www\.\S+", " ", text)
    for pattern, replacement in CONTRACTIONS:
        text = re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)
    text = re.sub(r"'s\b", "", text)              # remaining 's = possessive
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9\s]", " ", text)      # keep digits
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

def split_sentences(text):
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    text = re.sub(r"\b(Mr|Mrs|Ms|Dr|St|Jr|Sr)\.", r"\1<DOT>", text)   # mask, don't delete
    text = text.replace("U.S.", "U<DOT>S<DOT>")
    parts = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])[\"'”’]?\s+(?=[A-Z\"'“‘(])", text)
    return [p.replace("<DOT>", ".").strip() for p in parts if p.strip()]

# Unit tests
assert clean_text("We can't stop") == "we cannot stop"
assert clean_text("Freedom isn't free") == "freedom is not free"
assert clean_text("the nation's future") == "the nation future"
assert split_sentences("Mr. Smith left. He came back!") == ["Mr. Smith left.", "He came back!"]

example = "Mr. Chief Justice, we can't forget 1776: freedom isn't free---it's earned!  Our task is not finished."
print("RAW      :", example)
print("CLEAN    :", clean_text(example))
print("SENTENCES:", split_sentences(example))

4. Tokenization and stop-word removal

Tokenization cuts the cleaned text into words. A regex does the job: [a-z]+ keeps runs of letters.

Stop words are very common words (the, of, and, to) that carry little topical meaning. Removing them makes counts and word clouds far more informative. Two points of care:

  • A domain list is added. Words such as shall, upon or mr appear in almost every address as ritual language.
  • Negations are protected for sentiment. The standard list contains not, no and never. For word clouds they are removed; for sentiment they are essential, so the sentiment model uses a second list that keeps them.
In [5]
# Negations and near-negations that sentiment analysis needs
NEGATIONS = {"not", "no", "never", "none", "nobody", "nothing", "nowhere",
             "neither", "nor", "cannot", "without"}

# Ritual words that appear in nearly every address
DOMAIN_STOPWORDS = {"shall", "upon", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "let", "us",
                    "must", "will", "would", "may", "also"}

# Counts / word clouds: standard list + domain list (negations removed too)
STOPWORDS_COUNTS = set(ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS) | DOMAIN_STOPWORDS | NEGATIONS

# Sentiment: same list, but negations are kept
STOPWORDS_SENTIMENT = (set(ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS) | DOMAIN_STOPWORDS) - NEGATIONS

def tokenize(text):
    """Cut cleaned text into lowercase letter-only tokens."""
    return re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text)

def remove_stopwords(tokens, stopwords):
    return [t for t in tokens if t not in stopwords]

def prepare(text, for_sentiment=False):
    tokens = tokenize(clean_text(text))
    stops = STOPWORDS_SENTIMENT if for_sentiment else STOPWORDS_COUNTS
    return remove_stopwords(tokens, stops)

print("COUNTS   :", prepare(example))
print("SENTIMENT:", prepare(example, for_sentiment=True))
assert "not" not in prepare(example) and "not" in prepare(example, for_sentiment=True)

COUNTS   : ['chief', 'justice', 'forget', 'freedom', 'free', 'earned', 'task', 'finished']
SENTIMENT: ['chief', 'justice', 'cannot', 'forget', 'freedom', 'not', 'free', 'earned', 'task', 'not', 'finished']

Stemming reduces words to a common root, so govern, governed and government are counted together. It is shown for illustration only; the analyses keep the original words because they are easier to read in clouds and charts.

5. Word frequencies and word clouds

A word cloud draws each word with a size proportional to its frequency. It is a quick visual summary, but it shows frequency, not meaning, so it is always paired with an exact bar chart. The functions below take any {word: weight} mapping, which is reused for the era comparison.

In [7]

def plot_cloud(freqs, ax, title, max_words=80):
    """Word cloud if the package is installed, otherwise a bar chart."""
    if HAS_WORDCLOUD:
        wc = WordCloud(width=800, height=450, background_color="white", max_words=max_words,
                       collocations=False, random_state=SEED).generate_from_frequencies(dict(freqs))
        ax.imshow(wc, interpolation="bilinear")
        ax.axis("off")
    else:
        words, vals = zip(*Counter(freqs).most_common(15))
        ax.barh(words[::-1], vals[::-1])
    ax.set_title(title)

def plot_bars(freqs, ax, title, n=15, xlabel="Count"):
    words, vals = zip(*Counter(freqs).most_common(n))
    ax.barh(words[::-1], vals[::-1])          # reversed so the top word is on top
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_title(title)

5.1 Comparing historical eras

The speeches are grouped into four eras. The boundaries follow major turning points in U.S. history; they are a modelling choice, so the notebook reports how many speeches fall into each.

Era Years Context
Era 1 1789–1859 Early republic, up to the eve of the Civil War
Era 2 1860–1932 Civil War, Reconstruction, industrialisation, World War I, up to the Great Depression
Era 3 1933–1988 New Deal, World War II, Cold War
Era 4 1989–2025 Post-Cold-War era

For each era the notebook lists its most distinctive words. Plain frequency would just return government and people four times. Instead it uses the weighted log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn, 2008): each word's frequency in one era is compared with its frequency in the other three, the corpus-wide frequency serves as a prior, and the result is a z-score, so rare words with weak evidence are damped down automatically. (Plain TF-IDF would be a poor choice here: with only four "documents", its inverse-document-frequency term has just four possible values.)

In [8]
ERAS = {                      # inclusive start, exclusive end
    "Era 1": (1789, 1860),
    "Era 2": (1860, 1933),
    "Era 3": (1933, 1989),
    "Era 4": (1989, 2100),
}
era_names = list(ERAS)

def era_of(year):
    for name, (start, end) in ERAS.items():
        if start <= year < end:
            return name
    raise ValueError(f"year {year} is outside all eras")

speeches["era"] = speeches["year"].map(era_of)

display(speeches.groupby("era").agg(speeches=("year", "size"), first=("year", "min"),
                                    last=("year", "max"), words=("n_words", "sum")).loc[era_names])

# One count vector per era (rows = eras, columns = words)
era_docs = [" ".join(w for toks in speeches.loc[speeches["era"] == e, "tokens"] for w in toks)
            for e in era_names]
cv = CountVectorizer(token_pattern=r"[a-z]+", lowercase=False)
M = cv.fit_transform(era_docs).toarray().astype(float)
vocab = np.array(cv.get_feature_names_out())
total = M.sum(axis=0)

ALPHA0 = 500                              # strength of the prior (in pseudo-counts)
prior = ALPHA0 * total / total.sum()

def log_odds_z(i, min_count=5):
    """z-score of each word's log-odds in era i versus the other eras (Monroe et al. 2008)."""
    a, b = M[i], total - M[i]
    n_a, n_b, a0 = a.sum(), b.sum(), prior.sum()
    la = np.log((a + prior) / (n_a + a0 - a - prior))
    lb = np.log((b + prior) / (n_b + a0 - b - prior))
    z = (la - lb) / np.sqrt(1 / (a + prior) + 1 / (b + prior))
    z[total < min_count] = -np.inf        # ignore words seen fewer than 5 times in the corpus
    return z

distinct = {}
for i, e in enumerate(era_names):
    z = log_odds_z(i)
    top = np.argsort(z)[::-1][:40]
    distinct[e] = {vocab[j]: float(z[j]) for j in top if z[j] > 0}

display(pd.DataFrame({e: pd.Series(list(d)[:12]) for e, d in distinct.items()}))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))
for ax, e in zip(axes.ravel(), era_names):
    plot_cloud(distinct[e], ax, f"Most distinctive words: {e}", max_words=40)
finish("04_era_distinctive_words")

The lists should echo what each period was about (founding-era institutions, the Union and the Civil War, the Depression and the Cold War, recent themes). Because each era is pooled into one text, a word can be distinctive because one long speech repeats it; the table is a guide to themes, not a count of speeches.

6. How has speaking style changed?

Three simple measures per speech:

  • Average sentence length (words per sentence).
  • Lexical diversity: the share of distinct words among the first 500 cleaned tokens. A fixed length makes long and short speeches comparable; speeches shorter than 500 tokens are left out (NaN).
  • "We" versus "I": pronouns per 1,000 tokens. A rising we suggests a more collective tone. clean_text expands we're / we'll / I'm / I'd, so those are counted too.

The lines show a 5-speech rolling average on top of the individual speeches. Each trend is then tested with a Spearman rank correlation against the year (robust to outliers and non-linear trends).

In [9]
def words_raw(text):
    """Words as written (keeps contractions as one word), used for sentence length."""
    return re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+(?:['’][A-Za-z]+)?", text)

def avg_sentence_length(text):
    lengths = [len(words_raw(s)) for s in split_sentences(text)]
    return float(np.mean(lengths)) if lengths else np.nan

def lexical_diversity(text, n=500):
    tokens = tokenize(clean_text(text))
    if len(tokens) < n:
        return np.nan
    return len(set(tokens[:n])) / n

def pronoun_rates(text):
    tokens = tokenize(clean_text(text))
    if not tokens:
        return np.nan, np.nan
    scale = 1000 / len(tokens)
    return tokens.count("we") * scale, tokens.count("i") * scale

style = speeches[["fileid", "year"]].copy()
style["avg_sentence_len"] = speeches["text"].map(avg_sentence_length)
style["lexical_div"] = speeches["text"].map(lexical_diversity)
pron = speeches["text"].map(pronoun_rates)
style["we_per_1000"] = pron.map(lambda p: p[0])
style["i_per_1000"] = pron.map(lambda p: p[1])

for col in ["avg_sentence_len", "lexical_div", "we_per_1000", "i_per_1000"]:
    style[col + "_roll"] = style[col].rolling(5, center=True, min_periods=3).mean()

def draw(ax, col, label, color):
    ax.scatter(style["year"], style[col], s=18, alpha=0.35, color=color)
    ax.plot(style["year"], style[col + "_roll"], lw=2.5, color=color, label=label)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 10), sharex=True)
draw(axes[0], "avg_sentence_len", "5-speech average", "tab:blue")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Words per sentence"); axes[0].set_title("Average sentence length")
draw(axes[1], "lexical_div", "5-speech average", "tab:green")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Distinct / 500 words"); axes[1].set_title("Lexical diversity (first 500 tokens)")
draw(axes[2], "we_per_1000", "we", "tab:red")
draw(axes[2], "i_per_1000", "I", "tab:gray")
axes[2].set_ylabel("Per 1,000 tokens"); axes[2].set_title('"We" versus "I"')
axes[2].legend(); axes[2].set_xlabel("Year")
finish("05_style_over_time")

# Trend tests: Spearman correlation between the measure and the year
trend_rows = []
for col, label in [("avg_sentence_len", "Sentence length"), ("lexical_div", "Lexical diversity"),
                   ("we_per_1000", "'We' rate"), ("i_per_1000", "'I' rate")]:
    d = style[["year", col]].dropna()
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(d["year"], d[col])
    trend_rows.append({"measure": label, "spearman_rho": rho, "p_value": p, "n_speeches": len(d)})
trends = pd.DataFrame(trend_rows).set_index("measure")
display(trends.assign(p_value=trends["p_value"].map("{:.1e}".format)))

alpha_adj = 0.05 / len(trends)            # Bonferroni correction for 4 tests
for measure, r in trends.iterrows():
    direction = "rises" if r["spearman_rho"] > 0 else "falls"
    verdict = "significant" if r["p_value"] < alpha_adj else "not significant"
    print(f"{measure:18s} {direction} over time (rho = {r['spearman_rho']:+.2f}, {verdict} at the Bonferroni level {alpha_adj:.4f})")

Caveats. The ends of the rolling lines rest on only 3–4 speeches, so early peaks can reflect a few outliers. With 500 tokens per speech, lexical diversity is also sensitive to topic and to deliberate repetition (rhetorical anaphora lowers it). The tests show that style changed, not why; a shift from written to broadcast delivery, for instance, is one plausible driver that this data cannot isolate.

7. Sentiment scoring with VADER

Unit of analysis. A whole speech mixes many moods, so each speech is cut into passages of three consecutive sentences (passages with fewer than 8 words are dropped). This gives many more examples for the machine-learning model and still keeps enough context for sentiment. Section 7.2 checks that the conclusions do not hinge on this choice.

VADER relies on capitalisation and punctuation, so it runs on the raw passage, not the cleaned one. The usual cut-offs turn the compound score into a label:

Compound score Label
≥ 0.05 positive
≤ −0.05 negative
in between neutral
In [10]
sia = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()

def make_passages(text, size=3, min_words=8):
    """Cut a speech into passages of `size` consecutive sentences (no overlap)."""
    sents = split_sentences(text)
    passages = []
    for i in range(0, len(sents), size):
        passage = " ".join(sents[i:i + size])
        if len(words_raw(passage)) >= min_words:
            passages.append(passage)
    return passages

def label_from_compound(c):
    if c >= 0.05:
        return "positive"
    if c <= -0.05:
        return "negative"
    return "neutral"

def score_passages(size=3, min_words=8):
    rows = []
    for fid, year, text in zip(speeches["fileid"], speeches["year"], speeches["text"]):
        for k, passage in enumerate(make_passages(text, size, min_words)):
            c = sia.polarity_scores(passage)["compound"]          # raw passage, not cleaned
            rows.append({"pid": f"{fid}#{k}", "fileid": fid, "year": year, "passage_id": k,
                         "text": passage, "compound": c, "label": label_from_compound(c)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

passages_df = score_passages(PASSAGE_SENTENCES)
passages_df["era"] = passages_df["year"].map(era_of)

print(len(passages_df), "passages from", passages_df["fileid"].nunique(), "speeches")
print(passages_df["label"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3).to_string())
print(f"\nMean compound: {passages_df['compound'].mean():.3f} | "
      f"{(passages_df['compound'].abs() > 0.9).mean():.1%} of passages have |compound| > 0.9 (VADER saturates on longer texts)")

7.1 Sentiment over time and across eras

The unit of comparison is the speech (60 observations), not the passage (about 1,800 observations), because passages from one speech are not independent. For each speech two summaries are computed: the share of negative passages and the mean compound score. Era means come with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (resampling speeches), and a Kruskal–Wallis test asks whether the four eras differ at all.

In [11]
by_speech = (passages_df.groupby(["fileid", "year"])
             .agg(neg_share=("label", lambda s: (s == "negative").mean()),
                  mean_compound=("compound", "mean"),

             .reset_index().sort_values("year").reset_index(drop=True))
by_speech["era"] = by_speech["year"].map(era_of)

for col in ["neg_share", "mean_compound"]:
    by_speech[col + "_roll"] = by_speech[col].rolling(5, center=True, min_periods=3).mean()

# Linear-time trend (Spearman) at speech level
rho_mc, p_mc = stats.spearmanr(by_speech["year"], by_speech["mean_compound"])
rho_ns, p_ns = stats.spearmanr(by_speech["year"], by_speech["neg_share"])
print(f"Mean compound vs year : rho = {rho_mc:+.2f}, p = {p_mc:.3g}")
print(f"Negative share vs year: rho = {rho_ns:+.2f}, p = {p_ns:.3g}")

# Era comparison with bootstrap CIs (resampling speeches) and Kruskal-Wallis tests
def boot_ci(values, B=4000, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    means = rng.choice(v, size=(B, len(v)), replace=True).mean(axis=1)
    return np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])

rows = []
for e in era_names:
    d = by_speech[by_speech["era"] == e]
    mc_lo, mc_hi = boot_ci(d["mean_compound"])
    ns_lo, ns_hi = boot_ci(d["neg_share"])
    rows.append({"era": e, "n_speeches": len(d),
                 "mean_compound": d["mean_compound"].mean(), "mc_lo": mc_lo, "mc_hi": mc_hi,
                 "neg_share": d["neg_share"].mean(), "ns_lo": ns_lo, "ns_hi": ns_hi})
era_summary = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("era")
display(era_summary)

_, p_kw_mc = stats.kruskal(*[by_speech.loc[by_speech["era"] == e, "mean_compound"] for e in era_names])
_, p_kw_ns = stats.kruskal(*[by_speech.loc[by_speech["era"] == e, "neg_share"] for e in era_names])
print(f"Kruskal-Wallis across eras: mean compound p = {p_kw_mc:.3g} | negative share p = {p_kw_ns:.3g}")

How to read this. If the confidence intervals of neighbouring eras overlap heavily and the Kruskal–Wallis p-value is large, the honest conclusion is "no reliable era difference". A small p-value says the eras differ somewhere, not which pairs differ, and with 60 speeches the test has limited power. VADER caveat: it was designed for informal modern text, and archaic or formal language may be scored less reliably, especially in the earliest speeches. A drift in mean compound can also come from VADER saturating on long passages (many scores near +1) rather than from real mood change, which is why the share of negative passages is reported alongside it.

7.2 Sensitivity: does the passage size change the story?

The choice of three sentences per passage is arbitrary. The same analysis is repeated with 1, 3 and 5 sentences per passage. If conclusions flip with the window size, they are artefacts of the method.

In [13]
def show_extremes(df, n=3, width=100, max_chars=450):
    for title, part in [("MOST POSITIVE", df.nlargest(n, "compound")),
                        ("MOST NEGATIVE", df.nsmallest(n, "compound"))]:
        print("=" * 70); print(title); print("=" * 70)
        for _, row in part.iterrows():
            text = row["text"]
            if len(text) > max_chars:
                text = text[:max_chars].rsplit(" ", 1)[0] + " ..."
            print(f"[{row['year']}, passage {row['passage_id']}]  compound = {row['compound']:+.3f}")
            print(textwrap.fill(text, width=width)); print()

8. Human validation of the sentiment labels

Every sentiment result so far inherits VADER's judgment. The honest way to measure how far to trust it is a blind human check. This section does two things:

  1. Creates a stratified sample of 30 positive, 30 neutral and 30 negative passages (by VADER label) and writes it to validation_to_label.csv with an empty human_label column. The VADER label is not in that file, so labelling is blind. It is kept in validation_key.csv.
  2. Evaluates the labels if you have filled the column in: accuracy per VADER class, Cohen's κ (agreement beyond chance) and a confusion matrix.

To complete it (about 15 minutes): open validation_to_label.csv, write positive, neutral or negative for each passage using your own judgment of its stance (is the speaker expressing something hopeful or something grim?), save, and re-run the two cells below. Existing files are never overwritten, so your labels are safe. Until then the notebook runs normally and skips the numbers.

Because the sample is stratified (equal class sizes), overall accuracy on it is not the accuracy on the real corpus, which is about 78% positive. The per-class agreement figures are free of that distortion.

9. A machine-learning sentiment model

Task. Predict a passage's sentiment class from its words alone.

Why do this if VADER already scores the text? (a) It tests whether the sentiment is predictable from vocabulary. (b) The trained model can read texts without the lexicon. (c) Its coefficients show which words push a passage toward each class, including words the lexicon does not know.

Design

  • Features: TF-IDF of single words and word pairs, with negations kept (Section 4). Vectorisation happens inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so each fold learns its vocabulary only from its own training data.
  • Split by speech, not by passage (GroupKFold): every speech stays entirely on one side.
  • Metric: macro-F1 (average F1 over the classes), because the classes are unbalanced and accuracy would hide poor performance on the small ones.
  • Baseline: a classifier that always predicts the most frequent class.

9.1 Why the task is reduced to two classes

In [18]
passages_df["tokens"] = passages_df["text"].map(lambda t: " ".join(prepare(t, for_sentiment=True)))

def make_model(clf):
    return Pipeline([
        ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(token_pattern=r"[a-z]+", lowercase=False,
                                  ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=3, sublinear_tf=True)),
        ("clf", clf),
    ])

cv5 = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)       # deterministic: speeches are assigned to folds by size

print(passages_df["label"].value_counts().to_string(), "\n")
res3 = cross_validate(make_model(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced")),
                      passages_df["tokens"], passages_df["label"], groups=passages_df["fileid"],
                      cv=cv5, scoring=["f1_macro"])
print(f"Three-class logistic regression: macro-F1 = {res3['test_f1_macro'].mean():.3f}")
print("Neutral is only a few percent of the passages, so the model has almost nothing to learn it from.")
print("The task is therefore reduced to negative vs positive (neutral passages are dropped).")

9.3 Tuning the decision threshold without cheating

Logistic regression returns a probability of "negative". The default cut-off of 0.5 usually finds too few negative passages, so the cut-off is tuned for macro-F1. Choosing it on the same predictions that are then scored gives an optimistic result, so the tuning is nested: inside each outer training set, the threshold is chosen from inner out-of-fold probabilities, and the outer test fold is scored with that threshold without ever having influenced it.

In [20]
THRESH_GRID = np.round(np.arange(0.20, 0.81, 0.05), 2)
def lr_model():
    return make_model(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"))

def pick_threshold(X, y, groups, n_splits=4):
    """Choose the threshold that maximises macro-F1 on inner out-of-fold probabilities."""
    p = cross_val_predict(lr_model(), X, y, groups=groups, cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=n_splits),
                          method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
    scores = [f1_score(y, (p >= t).astype(int), average="macro") for t in THRESH_GRID]
    return float(THRESH_GRID[int(np.argmax(scores))])

p_oof = np.zeros(len(yb))
pred_nested = np.zeros(len(yb), dtype=int)
chosen = []
for train_idx, test_idx in GroupKFold(n_splits=5).split(Xb, yb, gb):
    t = pick_threshold(Xb.iloc[train_idx], yb.iloc[train_idx], gb.iloc[train_idx])
    fitted = lr_model().fit(Xb.iloc[train_idx], yb.iloc[train_idx])
    p_oof[test_idx] = fitted.predict_proba(Xb.iloc[test_idx])[:, 1]
    pred_nested[test_idx] = (p_oof[test_idx] >= t).astype(int)
    chosen.append(t)

pred_default = (p_oof >= 0.5).astype(int)
f1_default = f1_score(yb, pred_default, average="macro")
f1_nested = f1_score(yb, pred_nested, average="macro")
ap = average_precision_score(yb, p_oof)
auc = roc_auc_score(yb, p_oof)

print(f"Thresholds chosen in the 5 outer folds: {chosen}")
print(f"Macro-F1 at the default 0.5 threshold : {f1_default:.3f}")
print(f"Macro-F1 with nested tuned threshold  : {f1_nested:.3f}   (honest estimate)")
print(f"Threshold-free: average precision = {ap:.3f} (a random model scores {prevalence:.3f}), ROC AUC = {auc:.3f}\n")
print(classification_report(yb, pred_nested, target_names=["positive", "negative"]))

prec, rec, _ = precision_recall_curve(yb, p_oof)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
ax.plot(rec, prec, lw=2, label=f"Logistic regression (AP = {ap:.2f})")
ax.axhline(prevalence, color="gray", ls="--", label=f"Random model ({prevalence:.2f})")
ax.set_xlabel("Recall (negative passages found)"); ax.set_ylabel("Precision"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Precision-recall curve (out-of-fold)")
finish("08_precision_recall")

9.4 Does the model generalise across time?

Grouped cross-validation mixes eras in training and test sets. A harder and more realistic test: train only on speeches before 1933 and test on speeches from 1933 on. Vocabulary drifts over time, so a model that only works within an era would fail here.

p_late = fitted_early.predict_proba(Xb[~early])[:, 1]
pred_late = (p_late >= t_early).astype(int)

f1_late = f1_score(yb[~early], pred_late, average="macro")
f1_late_cv = f1_score(yb[~early], pred_nested[~early], average="macro")   # same test passages, mixed-era training
ap_late = average_precision_score(yb[~early], p_late)

9.5 What does the model learn, and how much is just VADER's dictionary?

The labels come from VADER's lexicon, so a good model should largely rediscover that lexicon. The cell below measures it: the share of the model's strongest words that VADER already knows. The words the model finds that VADER does not know are the interesting part: they are vocabulary specific to this genre that carries sentiment in these speeches.

In [22]
final = lr_model().fit(Xb, yb)
vocab_b = np.array(final.named_steps["tfidf"].get_feature_names_out())
coef = final.named_steps["clf"].coef_[0]
order = np.argsort(coef)                                    # most "positive-class" first
is_unigram = np.array([" " not in w for w in vocab_b])

def top_unigrams(idx_order, n):
    out = [vocab_b[j] for j in idx_order if is_unigram[j]]
    return out[:n]

neg_top = top_unigrams(order[::-1], 60)      # strongest words pushing toward "negative"
pos_top = top_unigrams(order, 60)            # strongest words pushing toward "positive"
lexicon = sia.lexicon

share_neg = np.mean([w in lexicon for w in neg_top[:30]])
share_pos = np.mean([w in lexicon for w in pos_top[:30]])
print(f"Top-30 'negative' words found in VADER's lexicon: {share_neg:.0%}")
print(f"Top-30 'positive' words found in VADER's lexicon: {share_pos:.0%}\n")
print("NEGATIVE, strongest words :", ", ".join(neg_top[:20]))
print("POSITIVE, strongest words :", ", ".join(pos_top[:20]))
print("\nNEGATIVE words VADER does not know:", ", ".join([w for w in neg_top if w not in lexicon][:15]))
print("POSITIVE words VADER does not know:", ", ".join([w for w in pos_top if w not in lexicon][:15]))

How the findings answer the questions

  1. Vocabulary. The log-odds lists show what each era talked about; the word clouds make the same point visually. Because eras are pooled texts, treat them as themes, not as statistics about individual speeches.
  2. Style. The trend tests say which of the three style measures changed monotonically. A measure that is not significant is an equally valid result: it says the data show no reliable change.
  3. Sentiment. The tone is dominated by the positive class, which is a property of the genre (ceremonial, unifying speeches) and partly of VADER's tendency to saturate. Whether eras differ should be read from the confidence intervals and the Kruskal–Wallis test, together with the sensitivity table, not from the point estimates alone.
  4. Model. The model beats the baseline and the threshold-free metrics show it ranks passages well above chance, but because the labels come from VADER's dictionary, much of what it learns is that dictionary. The share of top words found in the lexicon quantifies this.
  5. Trust in the labels. The human check (once completed) is the only evidence in this notebook about accuracy against real human judgment.

Limitations

  • Labels are model output, not ground truth. VADER was built for informal modern text. Formal and archaic language, rhetorical negation and long ceremonial sentences are known weak spots. The human sample is small (90 passages, one labeller, so no inter-annotator agreement) and stratified.
  • One speech per observation, 60 observations. Tests on era differences and trends have limited power; p-values are descriptive, not proof of causes.
  • Era boundaries are a judgment call. Different cut-points could move individual speeches between eras.
  • Passages of 3 sentences are arbitrary. Section 7.2 checks sensitivity but cannot remove the choice.
  • Style measures are crude. Sentence length depends on the sentence splitter; lexical diversity on a 500-token window; "we" counts do not distinguish "we, the people" from "we will".
  • Written text, not spoken delivery. The corpus has the prepared texts, not what was actually said.

Next steps

  • Label more passages with two annotators and report inter-annotator agreement.
  • Compare VADER with a transformer sentiment model or a domain-adapted lexicon; check where they disagree.
  • Add topic modelling (LDA or embeddings + clustering) to track themes and their sentiment over time.
  • Study individual presidents (e.g. wartime vs peacetime inaugurals) rather than only eras.
